extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining whether patent claims recite statutory subject matter and whether they are directed to judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) using the MPEP Step 1 / Step 2A (two-prong) framework and preparing appropriate rejections or recommendations for amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be made after determining what the inventor has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). In the flowchart (MPEP § 2106, subsection III) Step 1 determines whether the claim as a whole falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES) or does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI and mixed statutory/non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. It is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, that would narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory transitory signals example (machine-readable media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a product has a physical or tangible form, it may not fall within a statutory category; a transitory signal does not possess concrete structure that would qualify as a device or part under machine, a manufacture, or a composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: machine readable media BRI can encompass propagating electrical or electromagnetic signals. A claim to a computer readable medium that can be a compact disc or a carrier wave covers a non-statutory embodiment and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. See In re Nuijten and Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA for examples. If a claim is clearly not within the four categories (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made; use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to analyze the amended claim and recommend amendment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions – identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions to §101 include abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and laws of nature (also described as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no bright lines between types of exceptions and many concepts may fall under several exceptions. It is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. Judicial exceptions are excluded because monopolization of these basic tools could impede innovation; preemption is the underlying concern but not a standalone test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo framework required (Steps 2A and 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After Step 1, claims that fall within a statutory category must be analyzed under the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B) to determine whether they are directed to a judicial exception and, if so, whether they amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption concerns are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo framework. The absence of complete preemption does not by itself make a claim eligible; conversely, a preemptive claim may be ineligible. Use the Alice/Mayo test to evaluate eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry (Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks: does the claim recite (set forth or describe) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that the examiner believes may recite an exception and determine whether those limitations fall within a judicial exception. Distinguish between a claim that 'recites' an exception and one that merely 'involves' an exception. Example: a claim stating 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth a law of nature (recites an exception); a teeter-totter claim merely involves the law of the lever and does not recite the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry (Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks: do additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, then the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If they do not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis at Step 2B. Mere recitation of an exception triggers Prong One, but integration into a practical application is determined under Prong Two. Additional elements that are merely another judicial exception or do nothing more than recite conventional or generic implementation are insufficient to integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation requirement (Alice: 'transform the nature of the claim')
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim reciting a judicial exception to be eligible, the additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application of the judicial exception (either at Prong Two or in Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no additional elements beyond the judicial exception, the claim cannot be eligible. After making the appropriate rejection for lack of eligibility, recommend amendment if possible to resolve eligibility of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may recite multiple judicial exceptions; apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of the number of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless it is clear that a claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly for abstract ideas. If possible, treat limitations together as a single abstract idea for Prong Two and Step 2B. If exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature in one limitation and an abstract idea in another), for examination efficiency select one exception and conduct the analysis on that selected exception; if the claim integrates or amounts to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim should be considered eligible. If the claim does not amount to significantly more for the selected exception, consider ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas – enumerated groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate examination, abstract ideas are grouped into enumerated categories: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; (3) Mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent and shift examiners away from a pure case-comparison approach. Use the groupings to determine whether identified claim limitations fall within at least one grouping; if they do, the claim recites an abstract idea and proceeds to Prong Two. See MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2) for further discussion and examples of each subgrouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to determine if limitation recites an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine (1) the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) whether those limitations fall within at least one of the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limitation falls within a grouping, it is reasonable to conclude the claim recites an abstract idea and requires Prong Two analysis. If the limitation does not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea (barring rare circumstances discussed in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'recite' vs 'involve' an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'set forth' or 'describe' an exception recite it and require further eligibility analysis; claims that merely 'involve' an exception may be eligible and not require further eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms 'set forth' and 'described' indicate two ways an exception can be recited. Examiners should carefully distinguish recitation from mere involvement to avoid improperly treating eligible claims as directed to judicial exceptions. See examples such as Diehr and Mayo (set forth) vs teeter-totter (involves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere aggregation/addition of exceptions is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding one abstract idea to another, or having additional elements that merely recite another judicial exception, does not render the claim non-abstract or eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: RecogniCorp v. Nintendo (adding math to encoding/decoding insufficient); Genetic Techs. v. Merial (eligibility cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature itself). Examiners should find such claims require further analysis and not treat aggregation as a workaround to eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and business-method claims not categorically excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Software and business methods are not automatically abstract ideas or categorically outside §101's scope; the presence of an underlying mathematical calculation or relationship does not by itself doom the claim to abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent (e.g., Bilski, Thales Visionix, McRO, Enfish) to evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea or is a patent-eligible application. Examine the claim as a whole under the Alice/Mayo framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is the concern but not the test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's exclusionary principle is motivated by concern over preemption of basic tools; however, preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo two-part framework. The absence of complete preemption does not establish eligibility; use the Alice/Mayo framework to evaluate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practice to recommend amendment where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim fails Step 1 or lacks additional elements beyond an exception, it is a best practice for the examiner to recommend an amendment that would resolve eligibility of the claim, if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category or to integrate the exception into a practical application, proceed with examining such an amended claim and suggest amendments on the record.
